headline: Kazakhstan Celebrates Birth of First Wild Przewalski's Horses in 200 Years
meta_description: Two male foals born in August mark a turning point for the critically endangered Przewalski's horse and Kazakhstan's steppe restoration effort.
summary_short: Two male foals born in August at a reintroduction center in Kazakhstan are the first wild Przewalski's horses born on Kazakh soil in over 200 years.
body:
For the first time in more than two centuries, wild Przewalski's horses have been born on Kazakh soil. In late August, two male foals arrived at the Alibi Wild Ungulates Reintroduction Center—one on August 22 to a mare named Tessa, and another on August 31 to a mare named Umbra. Both inherited their bloodline from a stallion named Zorro. The births represent far more than a curiosity: they signal that this critically endangered species, extinct in the wild until 1996, is finally adapting to life on the Central Asian steppe after centuries of absence. "The birth of these two foals is important because it shows that the horses are adapting to this climate, to this territory," said Alyona Krivosheyeva, conservation director of the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan. "This is the proof of success of what we do."

Przewalski's horses, known locally as kertagy, are the world's only living wild relative of the domestic horse. They were hunted to extinction across Kazakhstan between the mid-18th and mid-19th centuries as the Russian Empire colonized the steppe for agriculture. Only captive populations in European zoos kept the species alive. Over the past three years, 22 horses have been translocated to Kazakhstan from Prague Zoo and Tierpark Berlin, grazing within the vast 489,000-hectare Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve.

These horses do more than roam: they reshape their habitat. Their grazing reduces wildfire risk, their hooves disturb soil to help new plants take root, and they disperse seeds across the grasslands. Conservationists aim to bring 40 horses to Kazakhstan—the minimum needed for a self-sustaining wild population. For now, the focus shifts to watching how these first foals born on Kazakh soil grow and thrive.
